This year marks the 150th anniversary of the bells being cast, the gift of the Countess of Ripon in memory of her husband.

Half-muffled before the requiem mass in celebration of the life and ordained ministry of Revd Carol Stone. Rung to mark the centenary of the 1/4th Battalion Oxford & Buckinghamshire Light Infantry leaving Writtle for France on 29th March 1915. The Ox & Bucks arrived in Writtle on 25th August 1914 having marched from Oxford over several days and were billeted around the village. They were made up to war establishment and spent time on long marches, range practice, trench digging and field day and night operations. The Ox & Bucks received orders to entrain for embarkation on 29th March 1915 and when 29 Officers and 991 other ranks marched out of the village the entire population was assembled round the Green to see them off and wish them well. They embarked on SS Onward at Folkestone bound for Bolougne eventually fighting on the Western front and being savagely mauled on the Somme in 1916.

Rung with the bells half muffled in memory of the following seven Lincoln men killed in the Great War during April 1915. Specially rung to commemorate the centenary of their deaths, We will remember them.
FREDERICK MARTIN, Private 9682, 1st Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Died of wounds 2nd April 1915, aged 19.
GEORGE DAWSON, Private 7744, “C” Company, 2nd Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 8th April 1915, aged 16.
JOHN WILLIAM HILEY, Lance Sergeant 14460, “C” Company, 2nd Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 20th April 1915, aged 37.
ERNEST JAMES LEAMY, Private 1680, “D” Company 1st/4th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 21st April 1915, aged 21.
HARRY LEE, Private 1680, “D” Company 1st/4th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 21st April 1915, aged 21.
WILLIAM WALTON ASHLEY, Lance Corporal 2174, 1st/8th Battalion, Sherwood Foresters, Nottinghamshire & Derbyshire Regiment. Killed in action 24th April 1915, aged 23.
THOMAS CROFT, Private 10342, 6th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Died 29th April 1915, aged 26.
When You Go Home, Tell Them Of Us And Say, For Your Tomorrow, We Gave Our Today.
Honourable age does not depend on length of days, nor is the number of years a true measure of life.
They are all commemorated on the City War Memorial on the High Street.

Rung for the 75th Anniversary of the Evacuation of Dunkirk and in memory of Lt Leslie Charles Green (uncle of the conductor) who was killed on 29th May 1940.

Lt Green was evacuated from the beaches and put aboard HMS Grafton (H89), a G-class destroyer. On the morning of 29 May, she stopped to rescue survivors from the destroyer Wakeful. While rescuing survivors from Wakeful off Nieuwpoort, Belgium, Grafton was struck in the stern by a torpedo from the German submarine U-62, killing the captain, another officer, 13 ratings and the Canteen Manager. The ship's back was broken, but she remained afloat long enough for all survivors to be rescued by the destroyer Ivanhoe and the transport Malines.
WW2 People’s War:

“A few small rowing boats kept coming in from the sea, loading with soldiers and rowing out to larger ships standing off in deeper water. Every now and then the beach was strafed by German aircraft but most enemy activity was concentrated on Dunkirk docks from which a huge pall of smoke drifted eastwards. We tied up alongside a destroyer, H.M.S Grafton and we were all transferred to this ship, a long weary process as other ships around us were attacked by the Luftwaffe. I was awakened by a loud explosion and looking to where the sound came from I saw the bow and stern of the ship that was in convoy with us, the destroyer H.M.S. Wakeful, disappear into the sea. She had been torpedoed amidships by a German E-boat and sank in a matter of moments with over 1200 lives. The Grafton fired at the E-boats and then stopped to look for survivors. About thirty minutes later just as our ship got under way there were two huge explosions as the Grafton was hit by two torpedoes, which blew off the stern of the ship. We lay, wallowing in the channel swell praying that the bulkheads would hold. If they had gone there would have been few survivors for there were no life jackets and most of the lifeboats and rafts had been damaged in the explosions. Everyone was ordered to keep still and to keep silent. I still remember the eerie silence, 1400 men making no sound, only the slap, slap as small waves lapped against the ship. There seemed to be two options now, either the-E boats came back and finished us off, or rescue”

Specially arranged and rung to mark the centenary of Lincoln born Leonard James Keyworth being awarded the Victoria Cross for his actions during the Great War.

On 25th/26th May 1915 at Givenchy, France, 21 year old Lance Corporal Leonard James Keyworth, of the 1st/24th (County of London) Battalion (The Queen’s), London Regiment, performed an act of bravery for which he was awarded the Victoria Cross.

Citation - “For most conspicuous bravery at Givenchy on the night of 25-26th May, 1915. After the assault on the German position by the 24th Battalion, London Regt, efforts were made by that Unit to follow up their success by a bomb attack, during the progress of which 58 men out of a total 75 became casualties. During this very fierce encounter Lance-Cpl Keyworth stood fully exposed for 2 hours on the top of the enemy's parapet, and threw about 150 bombs amongst the Germans, who were only a few yards away.”

Leonard James Keyworth was one of two Lincoln born men to receive the Victoria Cross during the Great War. He later achieved the rank of Corporal, but was sadly killed in action, at Abbeville, France, on 19th October 1915 at the age of 22 and is commemorated on the City War Memorial on the High Street.

Specially arranged and rung to celebrate the unveiling of the new Tank Memorial “Lincoln - Birthplace of the Tank” which stands on the roundabout at the end of Tritton Road (which is named after the Tank’s designer Sir William Tritton). The memorial is located just a few hundred yards from where the Wellington Foundry used to stand, which is where the first ever tank was built.

This quarter began at 10.30am exactly as the spitfires from the Battle of Britain Memorial Flight flew over the Church and over the memorial and was then rung while the official unveiling ceremony took place at 11.00am. The ceremony was attended by the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, the City Sheriff, members of the Civic Party, the Lord Lieutenant of Lincolnshire, members of the Tank Regiment along with the Tank Regiment Band.
This year marks the centenary of the first ever tank being built, which was built in Lincoln at the William Foster & Co Wellington Foundry which stood less than half a mile from this Church.
(Rung also for the Lincoln Diocesan Guild)

Rung especially remembering Foster’s Managing Director Sir William Tritton, his Chief Draftsman William Rigby and Major Walter Wilson of the War Cabinet, the designers and manufacturers of the original tank.

On this day one hundred years ago a bellringer from St. George’s Church, Jesmond was killed. We ring to celebrate his life and the ultimate sacrifice that he made.
Private Ernest Ranson Mundle.

Ernest was the son of Arthur Mundle and Annie of 42 St. George’s Terrace, Jesmond. He was born in Winlaton and left England on 3rd. May 1912 on The Empress of Ireland bound for Quebec in Canada he lived at Melville in Saskatchewan until enlisting at Camp Valcartier in Quebec. He served in the 5th. Battalion, Canadian Infantry. Ernest is buried in Bailleul Cemetery in France. Grave II.A.170. His name is recorded on the ringers plaque in this Cathedral.
Ernest Mundle we have remembered you

Rung half muffled to commemorate the life of Barry Albin-Dyer on the day of his funeral, and as the cortege passed the church.
The following is taken from Barry’s obituary in the Daily Telegraph:

Barry Albin-Dyer, who has died of cancer aged 64, was for 30 years the chairman of F A Albin & Sons, a venerable firm of funeral directors in Bermondsey, south London, which was tasked by the MoD with organising the repatriation and funerals of members of the Armed Forces who had died in Iraq and Afghanistan.

Clad in immaculate top hat and undertaker’s frock-coat and brandishing a cane, Albin-Dyer was a familiar sight at Bermondsey funerals, as well as at Wootton Bassett (and later Brize Norton), leading the cortege in the tradition known as “paging”.

It was Albin-Dyer who walked ahead of the flower-draped vintage Rolls-Royce containing the coffin of Jade Goody, the reality television star, in 2009. When the procession arrived at the market in Bermondsey where Jade Goody’s grandfather had kept a stall, Albin-Dyer released a white dove from a cage.
His pall-bearers also officiated at the funeral of 10-year-old Damilola Taylor in 2001.

The Mote Bell which hangs above the Guildhall was chimed 800 times to mark the 800th anniversary of Magna Carta and to celebrate Lincoln’s connections with Magna Carta. Rung as part of the National Ringing for Magna Carta and during the City’s Magna Carta Celebrations.
The bell was chimed in relays by members of The City of Lincoln Company of Civic Bell Ringers and by The Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln and the Lady Mayoress.

The Mote Bell is the oldest bell in Lincoln being cast in 1371 and was hung on top of the Guildhall above the Council Chambers with the sole purpose of being rung before every City Council Meeting to call the Council to gather, something which it has done for over 640 years and still does to this day.
What better way for Lincoln to “Strike a Blow for Democracy” than to have this bell ringing out for Magna Carta and for also The Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln to be involved in the chiming.

Rung on the front three during the unveiling of two commemorative paving stones remembering the two Lincoln born men, James Upton & Leonard James Keyworth, being awarded the Victoria Cross during the Great War, both being awared during May 1915. The ceremony took place at the Drill Hall with the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, the City Sheriff, members of the Civic Party and other City Dignitaries in attendance.

On 9th May 1915 at Rouges Bancs, France, 27 year old Corporal James Upton of the 1st Battalion, The Sherwood Foresters (The Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire Regiment) rescued the wounded while exposed to rifle and artillery fire, going close to the enemy's parapet. One wounded man was killed by a shell while the corporal was carrying him. When not actually carrying the wounded he was engaged in dressing and bandaging the serious cases in front of our parapet. For this action he was awarded the Victoria Cross.

On 25th/26th May 1915 at Givenchy, France, 21 year old Lance Corporal Leonard James Keyworth, of the 1st/24th (County of London) Battalion (The Queen’s), London Regiment, took part in a bomb attack, during which 58 men out of a total 75 became casualties. During this very fierce encounter Lance-Cpl Keyworth stood fully exposed for 2 hours on the top of the enemy's parapet, and threw about 150 bombs amongst the Germans, who were only a few yards away. For this action he was awarded the Victoria Cross.
James Upton and Leonard James Keyworth were the only two Lincoln born men to receive the Victoria Cross during the Great War.

Rung with the bells half muffled in memory of the following seven Lincoln men killed in the Great War during July 1915. Specially rung to commemorate the centenary of their deaths, We will remember them.
WILLIAM WOODCOCK, Private 2150, 1st/4th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Died 1st July 1915, aged 19.
JOHN HARRY CURTIS, Private 1609, 1st/4th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 14th July 1915.
ALBERT GOODSHIP, Private 2217, 1st/4th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 14th July 1915, aged 37.
WALTER AUCKLAND, Private 536, 1st/4th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 15th July 1915.
ALEXANDER GEORGE GOODHAND, Private 1777, 1st/4th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 15th July 1915, aged 23.
THOMAS SMITH, Private 10343, 6th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Died of wounds at Gallipoli 25th July 1915, aged 28.
SIDNEY GEORGE INCKLE, Private 2534, 1st/4th Battalion, Lincolnshire Regiment. Killed in action 26th July 1915, aged 18.
When You Go Home, Tell Them Of Us And Say, For Your Tomorrow, We Gave Our Today.
Honourable age does not depend on length of days, nor is the number of years a true measure of life.
They are all commemorated on the City War Memorial on the High Street.

This quarter especially remembers Barnard Reeve Beechey. He was one (the eldest) of eight brothers from the same family who went off to fight in the Great War and was the first of five to be killed, with only three returning home, one being crippled. Killed in the Battle of Loos, he charged to his death on 25th September 1915, aged 38. Just a few days before he was killed in September 1915, he wrote: "I really am all right and don't mind the life, only we all wish the thing was over." Amy Beechey their mother was presented to King George V and honoured by the King and Queen for her immense sacrifice, "It was no sacrifice, Ma'am," she told Queen Mary. "I did not give them willingly."

40 years ago, on Friday 24th October, 1975 a "peal" of 5088 Cambridge S. Major composed by John Carter was rung at this tower. Some 12 years later the composition was found to be false and the "peal" had to be withdrawn. Tonight matters have been put right with a true version of Carter's composition, which only differs in the final 3 courses, being successfully rung. Some interesting statistics:- same ringer on 4th, same ringer on 8th, same conductor and the same time as 40 years ago!

Rung with the bells half muffled to mark the centenary of the Battle of Loos at Hohenzollern Redoubt when the 4th & 5th Battalions of the Lincolnshire Regiment were the first over the top and virtually wiped out within the first 10 to 15 minutes. Many of the men killed were from the City and surroundings enlisting together in the Pals Battalion, with a total of 357 men from the Lincolnshire Regiment being killed and a total of 800 casualties overall. It was the greatest loss of Lincoln men on a single day during the Great War.

This quarter was rung immediately prior to a Service of Remembrance held at the City War Memorial on the High Street attended by the Lord Lieutenant of Lincolnshire, the Right Worshipful the Mayor of Lincoln, the City Sheriff, members of the Civic Party and the Freemen of the City along with various Forces Organisations, Associations, Veterans & Cadets. The quarter finished just before 1pm when a number of whistles were blown along the High Street marking the exact moment the Lincolnshire Regiment went over the top 100 years ago (being 2pm in France). This was followed by the 2 minutes silence.

Rung after Morning Service, at the invitation of the PCC to commemorate the Fauld Explosion when, at 11:11pm on 27th November 1944, 3670 tons of bombs exploded en-masse in an underground weapons storage facility. The force of the blast damaged every building in Hanbury and left a crater about 30m deep, 230m wide which covers an area of about 12 acres. It was heard as far away as Daventry and registered in seismographs in Switzerland. The force was about one fifth of that of the Hiroshima bomb making it one of the largest non-nuclear explosions, and the largest explosion on UK soil. The official death toll was 70 of which 18 have no known grave. Papers released in 1974 (the 30-year rule) indicated that the cause was a worker removing a detonator with a brass chisel rather than a wooden batten.

Specially arranged and rung to celebrate the centenary of Group Captain Gilbert Stuart Martin Insall being awarded the Victoria Cross on 7th November 1915 during the Great War. Group Captain Insall is buried in All Saints Churchyard and survived the Great War dying at the age of 77 on 17th February 1972.
Group Captain Insall’s Citation for the Victoria Cross

“For most conspicuous bravery, skill and determination, on 7 November 1915, in France. He was patrolling in a Vickers Fighting Machine, with First Class Air Mechanic T. H. Donald as gunner, when a German machine was sighted, pursued, and attacked near Achiet.

The German pilot led the Vickers machine over a rocket battery, but with great skill Lieutenant Insall dived and got to close range, when Donald fired a drum of cartridges into the German machine, stopping its engine. The German pilot then dived through a cloud, followed by Lieutenant Insall Fire was again opened, and the German machine was brought down heavily in a ploughed field 4 miles south-east of Arras.

On seeing the Germans scramble out of their machine and prepare to fire, Lieutenant Insall dived to 500 feet, thus enabling Donald to open heavy fire on them. The Germans then fled, one helping the other, who was apparently wounded. Other Germans then commenced heavy fire, but in spite of this, Lieutenant Insall turned again, and an incendiary bomb was dropped on the German machine, which was last seen wreathed in smoke. Lieutenant Insall then headed west in order to get back over the German trenches, but as he was at only 2,000 feet altitude he dived across them for greater speed, Donald firing into the trenches as he passed over.

The German fire, however, damaged the petrol tank, and, with great coolness, Lieutenant Insall landed under cover of a wood 500 yards inside our lines. The Germans fired some 150 shells at our machine on the ground, but without causing material damage. Much damage had, however, been caused by rifle fire, but during the night it was repaired behind screened lights, and at dawn Lieutenant Insall flew his machine home with First Class Air Mechanic T. H. Donald as a passenger."

He went to school in Beckenham and then attended Malvern College and Brasenose College, Oxford, where he studied law.  He met and married a Great Ryburgh woman called Muriel Smith and then in June 1915 he joined the East Kent Yeomanry and was sent to the Dardanelles. He was involved and seriously injured in an explosion at Helles and later died in hospital, in Malta, on November 5th, 1915.

’Twas chilly, and the slimy ropes
Did slide and slither in the frame:
All tipsy were the method hopes,
And the home calls outcame.
“Beware the Stedman my brave, brave one!
The points that stab, the places that catch!
Beware the Christmas Delight, and shun
Complacency that doth hatch!”
And, as the ringers rang with force,
The FireItOut, with eyes of flame,
Came whiffling through the third big course,
And chorlted as it came!
Dodge, two! Place, you! And through and through
The FireItOut went snicker-snack!
He left them dead, and then he fled
with ringers' spirits black.
“And hast thou slain the FireItOut?"
Their heads did drop and did declare
"O fractious day! Boo Hoo! Fired Out!"
A truly sad affair.

He was a true gent and always had a smile on his face and a kind word to say, he will be greatly missed. Our thoughts are with Kittie his wife and the rest of his family at this difficult time.
